scenes.kicker: F01 · Introduction to Financial Accounting · Module 2
scenes.head: The trial balance
scenes.sub: List every ledger balance in a debit or a credit column and the two totals should agree. Learn to prepare a trial balance, to use the gap between the totals to track down mistakes, and to recognise the errors that a trial balance in perfect balance can still hide.

segs.say: The trial balance. List every ledger balance in a debit or a credit column and the two totals should agree. Learn to prepare a trial balance, to use the gap between the totals to track down mistakes, and to recognise the errors that a trial balance in perfect balance can still hide.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Prepare a trial balance from ledger balances, listing accounts in chart order with each balance in its debit or credit column.
Explain why the two columns must agree, and what a balancing trial balance does and does not prove.
Identify errors a trial balance cannot detect: omissions, wrong accounts, reversals, compensating errors, and entries recorded twice or at the same wrong amount on both sides.
Locate an error from the difference between the column totals, using the halving test and the test for divisibility by 9.
Distinguish the unadjusted, adjusted and post-closing trial balances, and explain why none of them is a financial statement.

scenes.head: On 31 March Lantern Coffee Co.’s ledger holds sixteen accounts with balances.

segs.say: On 31 March Lantern Coffee Co.’s ledger holds sixteen accounts with balances. Before Ana Lim prepares March’s financial statements, she wants a quick test that nothing went wrong while fifteen journal entries became 31 postings. Checking every posting against the journal again would take an hour and could repeat the same slip. Instead she lists every account’s balance on one page, debit balances in one column and credit balances in another, and adds up both columns.

scenes.head: That list is a trial balance: every general ledger account with a balance, in chart-of-accounts order, each balance in its debit or its credit…

segs.say: That list is a trial balance: every general ledger account with a balance, in chart-of-accounts order, each balance in its debit or its credit column, with both columns totalled. If every journal entry had equal debits and credits and every posting copied them faithfully, the two totals must agree. If they don’t, something went wrong between the journal and the list, and the size of the gap is the first clue to what.
Work out the balance of every account in the ledger, on its normal balance side, as in the previous lesson.
Head the page with the business’s name, the title and the date. A trial balance is a snapshot of the ledger at one moment, so it carries a single date, not a period.
List the accounts in chart-of-accounts order, which for Lantern means by account number: assets, liabilities, equity and dividends, revenue, then expenses. Accounts with a zero balance are left out.

Write each balance in the column of its side: debit balances on the left, credit balances on the right. Usually that is the account’s normal side; a balance on the other side goes in the other column, flagged for investigation.
Add both columns and compare the totals.

scenes.head: Lantern’s ledger at 31 March gives the trial balance below.

segs.say: Lantern’s ledger at 31 March gives the trial balance below. It is prepared before the month-end adjusting entries of lesson 9, so it is Lantern’s unadjusted trial balance.
Lantern Coffee Co. · Unadjusted trial balance · 31 March 2026 (fictional case)

scenes.head: Read down the columns and the rules of module 2 reappear.

segs.say: Read down the columns and the rules of module 2 reappear. The debit column holds the assets, the dividends and the expenses; the credit column holds the liabilities, common stock and the revenues. Two lines deserve a second look. Dividends sits among the debits, but it isn’t an expense: it is a distribution to Lantern’s shareholder and will reduce retained earnings, not net income. Unearned Revenue sits among the credits, but it isn’t revenue: it is the $2,400 of catering Lantern still owes Harbor Tech.

scenes.head: Retained Earnings is missing because Lantern began on 1 March and has no profit from earlier periods.

segs.say: Retained Earnings is missing because Lantern began on 1 March and has no profit from earlier periods. In later months it will appear with its balance at the start of the period, because the current period’s profit stays spread across the revenue and expense accounts until the books are closed.

scenes.head: What the totals tell you

segs.say: What the totals tell you. Equal totals show that the ledger’s debits equal its credits. They don’t show that the right transactions were recorded, in the right accounts, at the right amounts. A trial balance tests the arithmetic of double entry, not the accounting.

scenes.head: The agreement is algebra, not luck.

segs.say: The agreement is algebra, not luck. Every journal entry has equal debits and credits, and posting copies them, so the ledger’s debit postings and credit postings have the same total: for Lantern’s March, $61,110 each. Write Dᵢ and Cᵢ for the debits and credits posted to account i. Its balance, counted as positive when it is a debit balance and negative when it is a credit balance, is Dᵢ − Cᵢ. Adding over every account:
Σᵢ (Dᵢ − Cᵢ) = Σᵢ Dᵢ − Σᵢ Cᵢ = 0 ⇒ total of debit balances = total of credit balances

scenes.head: Working out a balance nets the smaller side of an account against the larger, which removes the same amount from both columns.

segs.say: Working out a balance nets the smaller side of an account against the larger, which removes the same amount from both columns. Lantern’s Cash, Accounts Receivable and Accounts Payable netted $10,250, $3,000 and $1,000, $14,250 in all, which is why $61,110 of postings on each side becomes 61,110 − 14,250 = 46,860 in each column.

chapters.title: What a balancing trial balance proves, and what it doesn’t

scenes.head: Equal totals prove three things: the debits posted equal the credits posted, each balance was worked out and placed in a column consistently, and the…

segs.say: Equal totals prove three things: the debits posted equal the credits posted, each balance was worked out and placed in a column consistently, and the columns were added correctly. They prove nothing about whether the right things were recorded. A trial balance can balance and still contain errors, and some of the most expensive errors in accounting are exactly the ones it can’t see.

scenes.head: Bookkeeping courses in the British tradition give these undetectable errors standard names.

segs.say: Bookkeeping courses in the British tradition give these undetectable errors standard names. The Cambridge International AS & A Level Accounting syllabus for 2026–2028 lists errors of omission, commission, principle and original entry, reversals and compensating errors, and ACCA’s study material defines all but the last in the same terms. The American textbooks cited in this lesson describe the same mistakes without the labels. Here they are with Lantern examples, each a hypothetical mistake in March’s records.

Error of omission. A transaction left out entirely. If the utility bill of 31 March had never been recorded, Utilities Expense and Accounts Payable would each be $260 too low, and both columns would total $46,600.

Error of commission. The right amount on the right side, but in the wrong account of the same type. Posting March rent to Utilities Expense leaves Rent Expense at zero and Utilities Expense at $1,460; both are debit balances, so the totals don’t move. Posting an invoice to the wrong customer’s account is the same error inside a subsidiary ledger.

Error of principle. The right side, but the wrong type of account, which breaks an accounting principle. Suppose a $400 repair to the espresso machine were debited to Equipment instead of Repairs Expense: assets would be $400 too high and expenses $400 too low, and the totals would still agree.

Error of original entry. A wrong amount in the journal, posted faithfully to both accounts. If the 20 March wages had been journalised as $1,060 instead of $1,600, Wages Expense would be $540 too low and Cash $540 too high. Both are debit balances, so the debit column would still total $46,860.

Reversal of entries. The right accounts and amount with the debit and credit swapped. Recording Meridian’s $3,000 payment as a debit to Accounts Receivable and a credit to Cash would leave Cash at $20,650 and Accounts Receivable at $7,200, and both columns at $46,860.

Compensating error. Two or more errors whose effects cancel. If Wages Expense were overstated by $100 and Catering Revenue were also overstated by $100, both columns would rise to $46,960 and still agree.

Duplicated entry. A whole entry recorded twice adds equal debits and credits again. Journalising the $350 advertising payment twice would leave Advertising Expense at $700 and Cash at $26,300, with the totals unchanged.

scenes.head: Every one of these leaves a debit for every credit, and that common thread gives you a test for any mistake you meet: if it keeps debits equal to…

segs.say: Every one of these leaves a debit for every credit, and that common thread gives you a test for any mistake you meet: if it keeps debits equal to credits, the trial balance can’t see it. Finding such errors needs other checks: reconciling Cash with the bank statement and each control account with its subsidiary ledger, comparing balances with what you expected, and following cross-references back to the source documents.

chapters.title: Errors the trial balance does reveal

scenes.head: Anything that puts more on one side than the other shows up as a difference between the totals.

segs.say: Anything that puts more on one side than the other shows up as a difference between the totals. The common culprits leave differences with recognisable shapes:
One-sided errors and the difference each leaves (Lantern examples are hypothetical)

chapters.title: Using the difference to find the error

scenes.head: When the totals disagree, work through the checks in a fixed order, cheapest first.

segs.say: When the totals disagree, work through the checks in a fixed order, cheapest first. The sequence below follows the one in Edwards and Hermanson’s textbook (see the references), with one check, step 2, moved forward from its later list of causes:

scenes.head: The sequence below follows the one in Edwards and Hermanson’s textbook (see the references), with one check, step 2, moved forward from its later…

segs.say: Re-add both columns. Addition slips are common and quick to rule out.
Look for an amount equal to the difference: a balance missing from the list, or a journal line with a blank posting reference.

Halve the difference and look for that amount on the wrong side. A $300 debit listed as a credit makes the debit column $300 short and the credit column $300 long, a gap of $600. Start by checking that every balance sits on its normal side.
Divide the difference by 9. If it divides exactly, look for a transposition or a slide.

If none of that finds it, work backwards: compare every trial balance figure with its ledger account, recompute each ledger balance, check each posting against the journal through its posting reference, and finally check that each journal entry balances.

scenes.head: Notice which column is short.

segs.say: Notice which column is short. If the debit column is the smaller one, the error either understated a debit or overstated a credit, which halves the number of places to look.

chapters.title: Why transpositions and slides leave a multiple of 9

scenes.head: A transposition error swaps two digits: 54 written as 45, or 1,600 as 1,060.

segs.say: A transposition error swaps two digits: 54 written as 45, or 1,600 as 1,060. Take a two-digit amount with tens digit a and units digit b. Its value is 10a + b; with the digits swapped it is 10b + a. The difference is

scenes.head: which is always a multiple of 9, and the multiplier, a − b, is the gap between the two swapped digits.

segs.say: which is always a multiple of 9, and the multiplier, a − b, is the gap between the two swapped digits. When the pair sits further left, every place value is multiplied by 10, 100 or more, so the difference becomes 9(a − b) × 10^k. Writing 1,600 as 1,060 swaps the 6 in the hundreds place with the 0 in the tens place: 9 × (6 − 0) × 10 = 540, and indeed 1,600 − 1,060 = 540.

scenes.head: A slide error puts the decimal point in the wrong place, so every digit shifts: $350 recorded as $35, or as $3,500.

segs.say: A slide error puts the decimal point in the wrong place, so every digit shifts: $350 recorded as $35, or as $3,500. If the smaller figure is y, the larger is 10y and the difference is 10y − y = 9y. A slide of two places, $350 recorded as $3.50, gives 100y − y = 99y, also a multiple of 9.

scenes.head: A deeper reason covers every rearrangement of digits, not just neighbours.

segs.say: A deeper reason covers every rearrangement of digits, not just neighbours. Each power of ten is one more than a multiple of 9 (10 = 9 + 1, 100 = 99 + 1, 1,000 = 999 + 1), so any whole number equals a multiple of 9 plus the sum of its digits. Two numbers made of the same digits have the same digit sum (1,600 and 1,060 both have 7), so they leave the same remainder when divided by 9, and their difference is a multiple of 9. Adding or removing zeros, which is what a slide does, doesn’t change the digit sum either. When amounts include cents, apply the test to the difference in cents: $350 against $3.50 differs by 34,650 cents, which is 9 × 3,850.

scenes.head: A clue, not a proof

segs.say: A clue, not a proof. One whole number in every nine is a multiple of 9, so a difference divisible by 9 can come from an error that has nothing to do with digits, and every even difference passes the halving test. Two errors at once produce a difference that may match neither. Use each test to decide where to look first, and confirm by finding the actual mistake.

chapters.title: A trial balance is not a financial statement

scenes.head: A trial balance looks official, with a heading, a date and double-underlined totals, but it is an internal working document.

segs.say: A trial balance looks official, with a heading, a date and double-underlined totals, but it is an internal working document. It mixes accounts that belong on different statements: assets and liabilities from the balance sheet, revenue and expenses from the income statement, dividends from the statement of changes in equity. It has no subtotals, doesn’t show net income, and doesn’t separate current from noncurrent items. Its jobs are to check the ledger and to feed the statements; turning Lantern’s adjusted trial balance into financial statements is the subject of lesson 10.

scenes.head: Trial balance check

segs.say: Trial balance check: Σ Debit balances = Σ Credit balances.
Σ Debit balances: Total of the debit column: every account whose debits exceed its credits ($).
Σ Credit balances: Total of the credit column: every account whose credits exceed its debits ($).
It assumes this: Every journal entry balanced and was posted in full.
Necessary for correct records, not sufficient: errors that keep debits equal to credits pass.

scenes.head: Difference between the totals

segs.say: Difference between the totals: d = | Σ Debit balances − Σ Credit balances |.
d: The amount to be explained ($).
Note also which column is smaller: the error understated that column or overstated the other.

scenes.head: Amount on the wrong side

segs.say: Amount on the wrong side: x = d/2.
x: The amount posted to the wrong side, or the balance listed in the wrong column ($).
d: Difference between the totals ($).
It assumes this: A single error. In whole-dollar records an odd difference rules this out.

scenes.head: Difference left by swapping two neighbouring digits

segs.say: Difference left by swapping two neighbouring digits: d = 9 |a − b| × 10^k.
a, b: The two digits that were swapped.
k: Place of the lower digit: 0 for units and tens, 1 for tens and hundreds, and so on.
d: Difference the transposition leaves ($).
Any rearrangement of an amount’s digits leaves a multiple of 9, because the digit sum is unchanged.

scenes.head: Difference left by a slide

segs.say: Difference left by a slide: d = (10ⁿ − 1) y.
d: Difference the slide leaves ($).
y: The smaller of the correct and the recorded amounts ($).
n: Number of places the decimal point moved.
One place: d = 9y. Two places: d = 99y.

chapters.title: Example: Preparing a trial balance for a guesthouse

scenes.head: Preparing a trial balance for a guesthouse

segs.say: Saltmarsh Guesthouse, a fictional eight-room guesthouse, has these ledger balances on 30 September, in no particular order: Accounts Payable 2,310; Room Revenue 13,800; Cash 7,850; Wages Expense 6,900; Notes Payable 12,000; Equipment 21,500; Common Stock 10,000; Retained Earnings 4,190; Utilities Expense 1,320; Dividends 1,500; Accounts Receivable 1,240; Supplies 960; Laundry Expense 2,830; Unearned Revenue (guests’ deposits) 1,800. Prepare the trial balance totals.

scenes.head: Preparing a trial balance for a guesthouse

segs.say: Step 1. Decide each balance’s column from its normal balance. Debits: assets (Cash, Accounts Receivable, Supplies, Equipment), Dividends, and expenses (Wages, Utilities, Laundry). Credits: liabilities (Accounts Payable, Unearned Revenue, Notes Payable), equity (Common Stock, Retained Earnings) and Room Revenue.

Step 2. List them in chart order: assets, liabilities, equity, dividends, revenue, expenses. Retained Earnings appears because this isn’t the guesthouse’s first period: $4,190 is its balance at the start of September.

scenes.head: Preparing a trial balance for a guesthouse

segs.say: Both columns total $44,100, so the trial balance balances.

The guesthouse’s ledger is arithmetically consistent. That is all the agreement shows: a forgotten laundry bill or a deposit recorded as room revenue would pass unnoticed, so the owner still needs the reconciliations and reviews described in this lesson.

chapters.title: Example: Hunting a $540 difference in Lantern’s first draft

scenes.head: Hunting a $540 difference in Lantern’s first draft

segs.say: Suppose Lantern’s bookkeeper totals her first draft of the 31 March trial balance and gets debits of $46,320 and credits of $46,860. She has re-added both columns and they are correct. Find the error.

scenes.head: Hunting a $540 difference in Lantern’s first draft

segs.say: Step 1. The difference is 46,860 − 46,320 = 540, and the debit column is the short one: a debit balance is understated by $540, or a credit balance overstated by $540.

Step 2. Look for a $540 amount missing from one side: no balance or posting in March is $540. Halve it: 540 ÷ 2 = 270. No balance of $270 exists, and every balance sits on its normal side, so a wrong-column error is ruled out.

Step 3. Divide by 9: 540 ÷ 9 = 60 = 6 × 10. A slide would confuse $60 with $600, and there is no balance of either size. A transposition of neighbouring digits would have |a − b| = 6 in the tens and hundreds places (k = 1).

Step 4. Scan the balances for hundreds and tens digits that differ by 6. Only Wages Expense, 1,600, fits: 6 hundreds and 0 tens. The ledger says 1,600; the draft says 1,060. Correcting it raises the debit column to 46,320 + 540 = 46,860.

scenes.head: Hunting a $540 difference in Lantern’s first draft

segs.say: Wages Expense was copied onto the trial balance as $1,060 instead of $1,600. Corrected, both columns total $46,860.

Each test cut the search, and the direction of the difference cut it again. Notice the contrast with the error of original entry above: the same swap made in the journal, and posted to both Wages Expense and Cash, would have left the trial balance in perfect balance and the mistake invisible.

chapters.title: Example: Reviewing a trial balance that balances

scenes.head: Reviewing a trial balance that balances

segs.say: Kestrel Battery Installers, the fictional installer from lesson 3, keeps its books in accounting software, so its trial balance at 30 June balances. Before sending June’s figures to its bank, the controller reviews it and notes four things: Cash has a credit balance of $18,300; Accounts Payable shows $96,400 while the supplier ledger totals $97,050; Equipment rose by $2,750 in June although no equipment was bought, and Repairs Expense is $0 against a usual $2,000–$3,000 a month; and a suspense account holds a debit of $1,180. What does each suggest, and should the figures go to the bank yet?

scenes.head: Reviewing a trial balance that balances

segs.say: Step 1. Cash with a credit balance is an abnormal balance. If the bank statement confirms it, the account is overdrawn, which is in substance a short-term loan from the bank; if not, a receipt has been missed or a payment posted twice. Either way it must be explained before reporting.

Step 2. Accounts Payable is 97,050 − 96,400 = 650 below the supplier ledger. A bill posted to a supplier’s account but not to the control account would do exactly this; the posting references will show which.

Step 3. Equipment up by $2,750 with no purchase, and Repairs Expense unusually at $0, points to an error of principle: a repair debited to an asset. If so, June’s expenses are understated and its profit and assets overstated by $2,750.
Step 4. A suspense account is a temporary home for amounts awaiting investigation. A $1,180 balance means something hasn’t been classified yet, so June’s figures are incomplete until it is cleared.

scenes.head: Reviewing a trial balance that balances

segs.say: None of the four would make the totals disagree, yet each could misstate June’s figures. The controller should hold the report until all four are explained and corrected.

In software the arithmetic test is automatic, so the skill shifts to reading the trial balance critically: abnormal sides, amounts out of line with experience, control accounts that don’t reconcile, and holding accounts that aren’t empty. Lenders rely on these figures; a capitalised repair alone would make profit look $2,750 better than it was.

scenes.head: An interactive

segs.say: Post Lantern’s March entries one at a time and watch the trial balance build. After every entry the two columns agree, because every entry adds equal debits and credits. By 31 March both columns total $46,860. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: What does the difference suggest?

segs.say: Enter the difference between a trial balance’s two totals and see where to look first: an amount of that size missing from one side, half of it on the wrong side, or a transposition or slide when it divides by 9. Try 540, 600, 315 and 45, then an odd number that isn’t a multiple of 9. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: “The trial balance balances, so the books are right.”

segs.say: “The trial balance balances, so the books are right.”. Agreement proves only that debits equal credits. A transaction never recorded, rent posted to utilities, a repair added to equipment, an entry made twice or a wrong amount on both sides all leave the totals equal. Balancing is necessary, not sufficient.

scenes.head: “Dividends are an expense, so they belong with the expenses.”

segs.say: “Dividends are an expense, so they belong with the expenses.”. Dividends do sit in the debit column, next to the expenses, but they are a distribution of profit to shareholders, not a cost of earning revenue. They never enter net income; they reduce retained earnings. Grouping them with expenses would understate Lantern’s March profit by $300.

scenes.head: “A contra account is listed with its asset, so it goes in the debit column.”

segs.say: “A contra account is listed with its asset, so it goes in the debit column.”. A contra account has the opposite normal balance to the account it reduces. Lantern’s adjusted trial balance will include Accumulated Depreciation—Equipment with a credit balance of $200; it belongs in the credit column even though it is listed among the assets.

scenes.head: “Retained Earnings on the trial balance includes this period’s profit.”

segs.say: “Retained Earnings on the trial balance includes this period’s profit.”. Until the books are closed, the period’s revenue and expenses sit in their own accounts. The Retained Earnings figure on an unadjusted or adjusted trial balance is the balance at the start of the period; Lantern’s is zero in its first month.

scenes.head: “A difference divisible by 9 proves a transposition.”

segs.say: “A difference divisible by 9 proves a transposition.”. It is a lead, not proof. One whole number in nine is a multiple of 9 anyway, and a slide, or two unrelated errors, can produce one too. Confirm by finding the figure that doesn’t match the ledger.

scenes.head: “The trial balance is the balance sheet.”

segs.say: “The trial balance is the balance sheet.”. A trial balance lists every account, including revenue, expenses and dividends, with no classification or subtotals. It is a working document that feeds the balance sheet, the income statement and the statement of changes in equity; it isn’t any of them.

scenes.head: In accounting software a trial balance is a report you can run for any date, and it always balances: as ACCA’s study material for its Financial…

segs.say: In accounting software a trial balance is a report you can run for any date, and it always balances: as ACCA’s study material for its Financial Accounting exam notes, a computerised system will usually refuse to post an unbalanced journal entry. The error-hunting skills of this lesson still matter wherever figures are kept by hand or in spreadsheets, wherever balances are copied from one system into another, and in professional exams. Reviewing a trial balance that balances matters everywhere.

scenes.head: An experienced accountant reads a trial balance the way a doctor reads a set of test results, looking for anything outside the expected range.

segs.say: An experienced accountant reads a trial balance the way a doctor reads a set of test results, looking for anything outside the expected range. A typical review asks four questions:

scenes.head: A typical review asks four questions:

segs.say: Is every balance on its normal side? A credit balance in Cash means an overdraft; a debit balance in Accounts Payable means a supplier was overpaid or a payment was misposted; a debit balance in a revenue account means refunds exceed sales or something is wrong.

Does every balance make sense in size? Compare with last month, with the budget, and with what you know happened. Lantern’s Supplies shows $1,500, the cost of everything bought in March, though Ana knows much of it has been used. That isn’t an error; it is a sign that an adjustment is due (lesson 9).
Are the accounts that should be empty, empty? A suspense account, used to hold amounts while they are investigated, should be cleared before statements are prepared.
Do the control accounts agree with their subsidiary ledgers, and does Cash agree with the bank? These reconciliations catch many of the errors a trial balance can’t.

scenes.head: Scale doesn’t change the logic.

segs.say: Scale doesn’t change the logic. An airline or a university may have thousands of accounts, extracted from the general ledger by software, and its finance team still starts the month-end review by scanning the trial balance for abnormal and unexpected balances before anything goes into the financial statements. External auditors usually start from the client’s trial balance too, because it lists every account they may need to test and links the ledger to the published statements.

scenes.head: For a small business owner the trial balance is the last checkpoint before the numbers leave the building.

segs.say: For a small business owner the trial balance is the last checkpoint before the numbers leave the building. If Ana applies to Coastline Bank for the van loan she is considering (lesson 3), the bank will judge Lantern on statements built from its trial balance. A repair hidden in Equipment, or a supplier bill missing from Accounts Payable, would make Lantern look stronger than it is, and the trial balance’s agreement wouldn’t have warned her. The review would.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: A trial balance lists every ledger account with a balance, in chart order, each balance in its debit or credit column, at one date. The two columns must total the same.
They agree because every entry posts equal debits and credits. Lantern’s unadjusted trial balance at 31 March totals $46,860 on each side.

Equal totals test the arithmetic of double entry, not the accounting: omissions, commission and principle errors, reversals, duplicated entries, wrong amounts on both sides and compensating errors all pass.
Unequal totals point to one-sided errors. Look for the difference itself, for half of it on the wrong side, and, if it divides by 9, for a transposition or a slide.
Transpositions and slides leave multiples of 9 because numbers with the same digits have the same digit sum. The test is a clue, not proof.
Unadjusted, adjusted and post-closing trial balances are prepared at three points in the cycle. None is a financial statement.
In software the trial balance always balances, so its value lies in review: abnormal sides, unexpected sizes, uncleared holding accounts and unreconciled control accounts.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
